title: Scientific Integrity in Public Health Research: A Policy Analysis
summary: Establishes protections for state-funded public health researchers against political interference, mandates transparent research methodology and timely publication of findings, prohibits suppression or alteration of scientific conclusions for political purposes, and creates enforceable whistleblower protections for researchers who report violations.
text: Educational example, not proposed legislation. This document is provided by the SAFE Research Institute for educational analysis of how a policy approach might be structured. It is not a bill, and its inclusion here is not a recommendation to adopt any measure. This educational example examines an approach relating to scientific integrity; establishing protections for state-funded public health researchers; prohibiting political interference with scientific research and findings; mandating transparent research methodology; providing whistleblower protections; and providing for related matters. Section 1. Purpose and Findings (a) This example is premised on the following findings: 1. Sound public health policy depends upon the free, transparent, and impartial conduct of scientific research, unimpeded by political considerations or ideological pressure. 2. Concerns about political influence on the work of public health agencies have been the subject of significant public debate and of federal scientific-integrity policymaking, underscoring the importance of clear safeguards for research independence at every level of government. 3. Researchers employed by or funded through state agencies have reported instances of pressure to alter findings, delay publication of results, or refrain from investigating topics deemed politically sensitive, to the detriment of public health. 4. The suppression, alteration, or selective release of scientific findings for political purposes poses a direct threat to the health and safety of the public, as policymakers and health care providers rely on accurate and timely scientific evidence to inform decisions affecting millions of residents. 5. Multiple federal scientific integrity policies established between 2009 and 2022 demonstrated the feasibility and importance of institutional safeguards for research independence, and changes to federal scientific integrity frameworks have prompted interest in state-level approaches to research governance. 6. It is in the interest of the state to establish robust, enforceable protections for scientific integrity in public health research conducted with state funds or under state authority. (b) The purpose of this measure is to safeguard the integrity, independence, and transparency of public health research conducted by or on behalf of the state, to protect researchers from retaliation for adhering to scientific standards, and to ensure that the public and policymakers have access to accurate, timely, and complete scientific information. Section 2. Definitions As used in this measure: 1. "Covered agency" means any state agency, department, board, commission, or public institution of higher education that conducts, funds, or oversees public health research, including but not limited to the state department of health, the state environmental agency, and public universities. 2. "Covered researcher" means any individual who conducts public health research in whole or in part with state funds, under state authority, or as an employee or contractor of a covered agency, including principal investigators, co-investigators, research staff, laboratory personnel, and graduate research assistants. 3. "Department" means the state department of health or its successor agency. 4. "Inspector General" means the state inspector general, the inspector general of the relevant covered agency, or a designated independent entity as established under Section 7 of this measure. 5. "Political interference" means any action by an elected official, political appointee, or other non-scientific personnel that is intended to, or has the effect of, improperly influencing the design, conduct, analysis, reporting, or dissemination of public health research for reasons unrelated to scientific merit, methodological rigor, or legal compliance. 6. "Public health research" means systematic investigation, including research development, testing, evaluation, and dissemination of findings, designed to develop or contribute to generalizable knowledge related to the prevention of disease, promotion of health, or understanding of environmental, behavioral, or biological determinants of health. 7. "Retaliation" means any adverse employment action, including termination, demotion, suspension, reassignment, reduction in funding, denial of promotion, or other materially adverse change in the terms or conditions of employment or funding, taken against a covered researcher in response to protected activity under this measure. 8. "Scientific findings" means the data, analyses, conclusions, and recommendations resulting from public health research. 9. "Scientific Integrity Officer" means the individual designated under Section 3 of this measure. Section 3. Scientific Integrity Officer (a) Each covered agency shall designate a Scientific Integrity Officer who shall: 1. Be a senior-level employee with demonstrated expertise in scientific research methodology and ethics; 2. Report directly to the head of the covered agency on matters relating to scientific integrity; 3. Not be subject to removal except for cause, following notice and an opportunity to be heard; 4. Not hold any concurrent political appointment or serve at the pleasure of any elected official; and 5. Serve a fixed term of not less than four years, which may be renewed. (b) The Scientific Integrity Officer shall have the authority and responsibility to: 1. Develop, implement, and enforce a scientific integrity policy for the covered agency consistent with the requirements of this measure; 2. Receive and investigate complaints of political interference or violations of scientific integrity; 3. Issue findings and recommendations to the agency head, which shall be made public within thirty days of issuance; 4. Publish an annual report on the state of scientific integrity within the covered agency, including the number and disposition of complaints received; and 5. Coordinate with the Inspector General on matters involving potential violations of law. Section 4. Protections for Research Independence (a) No elected official, political appointee, or other non-scientific personnel shall: 1. Direct or coerce a covered researcher to alter, suppress, delay, or misrepresent scientific findings; 2. Prohibit or restrict a covered researcher from publishing, presenting, or otherwise disseminating scientific findings in peer-reviewed journals, at professional conferences, or through other customary channels of scientific communication; 3. Require pre-publication review of scientific manuscripts by political appointees or non-scientific communications staff for purposes other than ensuring compliance with applicable law regarding classified information, privacy, or intellectual property; 4. Remove or alter scientific content from agency websites, publications, or public communications without the written concurrence of the principal investigator or the Scientific Integrity Officer; 5. Prohibit the use of specific scientific terms, methodologies, or analytical frameworks in research documents or public communications for non-scientific reasons; 6. Terminate, reduce, or redirect research funding based on the anticipated or actual conclusions of the research rather than on scientific merit, programmatic relevance, or fiscal necessity; or 7. Interfere with the selection, appointment, or tenure of members of scientific advisory committees on the basis of the political implications of their scientific views. (b) Nothing in this section shall be construed to: 1. Prevent the exercise of legitimate supervisory authority over research conducted by covered agencies, including decisions related to research priorities, resource allocation based on programmatic needs, or compliance with applicable law; 2. Restrict the authority of covered agencies to establish policies governing conflicts of interest, human subjects protection, data security, or other matters unrelated to the suppression of scientific findings; or 3. Prohibit an agency head from requiring factual accuracy review of scientific communications by qualified scientific personnel prior to public release. Section 5. Transparent Research Methodology (a) Each covered agency shall adopt and maintain policies ensuring that: 1. All public health research funded by or conducted under the authority of the agency adheres to established standards of scientific methodology, including peer review, reproducibility, and transparent reporting of methods, data, and analytical techniques; 2. Research protocols, data sets, and analytical methods are made publicly available to the extent permitted by law, with appropriate protections for personally identifiable information, proprietary information, and ongoing investigations; 3. Research findings are published in a timely manner, and no scientific finding shall be withheld from publication for longer than twelve months from the completion of the research without a written justification approved by the Scientific Integrity Officer; 4. All public health research reports published by the agency include a clear description of the methodology, funding sources, potential conflicts of interest, and any limitations of the research; and 5. Covered researchers are permitted and encouraged to include their own professional interpretations and policy implications in scientific publications, clearly distinguished from official agency positions where appropriate. (b) The department shall establish and maintain a publicly accessible online repository of all public health research reports produced by covered agencies, including metadata sufficient to identify the research topic, investigators, funding source, and date of completion. Section 6. Whistleblower Protections (a) No covered agency or officer thereof shall take or threaten to take any retaliatory action against a covered researcher who, in good faith: 1. Reports a suspected violation of this measure to the Scientific Integrity Officer, the Inspector General, a member of the Legislature, or any other appropriate authority; 2. Refuses to engage in conduct that would constitute a violation of this measure; 3. Provides testimony or cooperates with an investigation under this measure; or 4. Exercises any right protected under this measure. (b) A covered researcher who is subjected to retaliation in violation of this section may: 1. File a complaint with the Scientific Integrity Officer or the Inspector General within one hundred eighty days of the retaliatory action; 2. Bring a civil action in a court of competent jurisdiction within two years of the retaliatory action; and 3. Obtain relief including: - (i) Reinstatement to the position held prior to the retaliation, or to an equivalent position; - (ii) Back pay with interest, and restoration of any lost benefits or seniority; - (iii) Compensatory damages for harm suffered as a result of the retaliation; - (iv) Reasonable attorneys' fees and costs of litigation; and - (v) Such other equitable relief as the court deems necessary to make the covered researcher whole. (c) In any proceeding under this section, a rebuttable presumption of retaliation shall arise if an adverse employment action is taken within twelve months of the covered researcher engaging in protected activity under this measure. The burden shall then shift to the covered agency to demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that the adverse action was taken for legitimate, non-retaliatory reasons. Section 7. Enforcement (a) The Inspector General shall have the authority to investigate complaints of violations of this measure, including political interference and retaliation, and to issue findings and recommendations. (b) A covered agency that is found to have violated this measure may be subject to: 1. A requirement to restore any suppressed, altered, or withdrawn scientific findings to their original form and make them publicly available; 2. Mandatory corrective action, including revision of policies and training of personnel; 3. Reporting to the Legislature and the Governor on the violation and corrective actions taken; and 4. Such other remedies as may be appropriate under applicable law. (c) An individual who knowingly and willfully directs or coerces a covered researcher to violate this measure, or who knowingly and willfully retaliates against a covered researcher in violation of Section 6, shall be subject to: 1. Disciplinary action, up to and including termination of employment; 2. Civil penalties of not less than five thousand dollars ($5,000) nor more than fifty thousand dollars ($50,000) per violation; and 3. Referral to the appropriate law enforcement authority if the conduct constitutes a criminal offense under other applicable law. Section 8. Scientific Integrity Advisory Board (a) There is hereby established a Scientific Integrity Advisory Board, composed of not fewer than seven members appointed as follows: 1. Three members appointed by the Governor, each of whom shall be a scientist with expertise in public health, epidemiology, or biomedical research and shall not hold any political office or appointment; 2. Two members appointed by the Legislature, one by the presiding officer of each chamber, each of whom shall be a scientist or ethicist with expertise relevant to scientific integrity; 3. One member appointed by the state's public university system, who shall be a tenured faculty member with an active research program in public health or a related discipline; and 4. One member who is a covered researcher, elected by covered researchers across the state's covered agencies. (b) The Board shall: 1. Review and provide recommendations on the scientific integrity policies of covered agencies; 2. Hear appeals from covered researchers who are dissatisfied with the disposition of complaints by a Scientific Integrity Officer; 3. Publish a biennial report assessing the state of scientific integrity in public health research across the state; and 4. Advise the Legislature on any legislative changes needed to strengthen protections for scientific integrity. Section 9. Periodic Review and Reporting (a) Each covered agency shall conduct an internal review of its compliance with this measure not less than once every two years and shall submit a report of its findings to the Scientific Integrity Advisory Board and the relevant committees of the Legislature. (b) The Scientific Integrity Advisory Board shall compile the agency reports and publish a comprehensive statewide assessment of scientific integrity, which shall be made available to the public on the department's website. Section 10. Severability If any provision of this measure, or its application to any person or circumstance, is held invalid, the invalidity does not affect other provisions or applications of this measure that can be given effect without the invalid provision or application, and to this end the provisions of this measure are severable. Section 11. Effective Date This measure shall take effect on [DATE], or upon passage and approval, whichever is later. Policy Considerations This model legislation represents one approach to establishing institutional protections for scientific research independence at the state level. Legislators considering this template should evaluate: - The balance between protecting researcher independence and preserving legitimate executive authority over agency priorities, resource allocation, and public communications - Whether whistleblower protections and civil penalty provisions may create unintended consequences, such as chilling legitimate supervisory feedback or encouraging frivolous complaints - Administrative costs of establishing and staffing Scientific Integrity Officers, advisory boards, and complaint investigation processes across multiple covered agencies - Fiscal impact on state budgets and healthcare systems - Compatibility with existing state statutes and regulatory frameworks The SAFE Research Institute presents this material as an educational resource and does not advocate for or against any specific legislative outcome. --- This document is provided by the SAFE Research Institute as an educational resource. It is not legal advice. It is offered to inform analysis and discussion, not to promote the adoption of any particular measure. Readers should consult qualified professionals regarding their existing statutory frameworks, constitutional provisions, and administrative procedures.

title: Pharmacist Immunization Authority: A Policy Analysis
summary: Permanently expands pharmacist scope of practice to administer all FDA-approved and FDA-authorized vaccines to individuals aged three and older without requiring a physician referral or prescriptive authority, codifying flexibilities first established under the federal PREP Act during the COVID-19 public health emergency.
text: Educational example, not proposed legislation. This document is provided by the SAFE Research Institute for educational analysis of how a policy approach might be structured. It is not a bill, and its inclusion here is not a recommendation to adopt any measure. This educational example examines an approach relating to the practice of pharmacy; expanding the authority of licensed pharmacists to administer vaccines; removing certain referral and prescriptive authority requirements; establishing training and reporting standards; and providing for related matters. Section 1. Purpose and Findings (a) This example is premised on the following findings: 1. Pharmacists are among the most accessible health care providers in the United States, with approximately ninety percent of Americans living within five miles of a community pharmacy. 2. During the COVID-19 public health emergency, the federal Public Readiness and Emergency Preparedness (PREP) Act and subsequent amendments authorized pharmacists nationwide to administer a broad range of vaccines to individuals aged three and older, demonstrating the safety and efficacy of pharmacist-administered vaccination on a large scale. 3. Public health analyses of the period of expanded federal authorization have reported that pharmacist-administered vaccinations expanded immunization access, particularly in rural and medically underserved communities. 4. Following the expiration of federal emergency declarations, multiple states have enacted permanent legislation codifying expanded pharmacist vaccination authority, and proponents point to improved access where such authority has been retained. 5. Unnecessary referral requirements and restrictive scope-of-practice limitations create barriers to timely immunization, disproportionately affecting populations with limited access to primary care providers. 6. It is in the interest of the state to permanently authorize licensed pharmacists to administer all FDA-approved and FDA-authorized vaccines, subject to appropriate training and reporting requirements, in order to maximize immunization access for all residents. (b) The purpose of this measure is to permanently expand the scope of practice of licensed pharmacists to include the administration of all FDA-approved and FDA-authorized vaccines to eligible individuals, thereby reducing barriers to immunization access and codifying the documented public health benefits of pharmacist-administered vaccination. Section 2. Definitions As used in this measure: 1. "Board" means the state board of pharmacy or its successor agency. 2. "Department" means the state department of health or its successor agency. 3. "FDA-approved vaccine" means any vaccine that has received full approval from the United States Food and Drug Administration for use in humans. 4. "FDA-authorized vaccine" means any vaccine that has received an Emergency Use Authorization from the United States Food and Drug Administration for use in humans. 5. "Immunization registry" means the statewide immunization information system maintained by the department for the purpose of recording and tracking vaccine administration. 6. "Licensed pharmacist" means an individual holding an active, unrestricted license to practice pharmacy in this state. 7. "Pharmacy intern" means an individual enrolled in an accredited school or college of pharmacy who is practicing under the direct supervision of a licensed pharmacist, as defined by the board. 8. "Qualified pharmacist" means a licensed pharmacist who has completed the training requirements set forth in Section 4 of this measure. 9. "Standing order" means a written protocol issued by a physician, the department, or the state health officer authorizing the administration of vaccines under specified conditions without requiring an individual patient prescription. Section 3. Pharmacist Vaccination Authority (a) A qualified pharmacist may order, administer, and provide consultation regarding any FDA-approved vaccine or FDA-authorized vaccine to individuals aged three years and older, without requiring: 1. A patient-specific prescription from a physician or other prescriber; 2. A referral from a physician or other health care provider; 3. A collaborative practice agreement with a physician, except as may be otherwise required by the board for specific classes of vaccines administered to individuals aged three through six years; or 4. Prior authorization from a health plan or insurer as a condition of vaccine administration. (b) A qualified pharmacist may administer vaccines to individuals aged three through six years pursuant to a standing order issued by the department, the state health officer, or a licensed physician, provided that the pharmacist has completed the additional pediatric training requirements established under Section 4(b) of this measure. (c) A pharmacy intern may administer vaccines under the direct supervision of a qualified pharmacist, provided that the pharmacy intern has completed the training requirements established under Section 4(a) of this measure. (d) Nothing in this measure shall be construed to: 1. Expand the authority of pharmacists to prescribe non-vaccine medications; 2. Limit the authority of physicians or other licensed health care providers to administer vaccines within their existing scope of practice; or 3. Affect vaccine requirements for school enrollment or other purposes established under existing state law. Section 4. Training Requirements (a) To qualify as a qualified pharmacist under this measure, a licensed pharmacist shall complete and maintain current certification in: 1. An immunization delivery training program accredited by the Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education (ACPE) that includes, at minimum: - (i) Evidence-based immunization guidelines, including the schedules recommended by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the American Academy of Pediatrics, and the American Academy of Family Physicians; - (ii) Vaccine storage, handling, and administration techniques appropriate for all approved routes of administration; - (iii) Recognition and treatment of adverse reactions, including anaphylaxis; - (iv) Patient screening, contraindication assessment, and informed consent procedures; - (v) Requirements for documentation and reporting of administered vaccines. 2. A current certificate in Basic Life Support (BLS) from the American Heart Association, the American Red Cross, or an equivalent nationally recognized provider. (b) A qualified pharmacist who administers vaccines to individuals aged three through six years shall complete not fewer than two additional hours of continuing education specifically addressing pediatric immunization, including: 1. Age-appropriate dosing and administration techniques for young children; 2. Pediatric-specific contraindications and precautions; 3. Communication strategies for caregivers; and 4. Recognition and management of adverse events specific to pediatric populations. (c) The board shall establish, by regulation, requirements for ongoing continuing education in immunization delivery as a condition of license renewal, which shall include not fewer than two hours of immunization-related continuing education per biennial renewal period. Section 5. Vaccine Administration Protocols (a) A qualified pharmacist administering vaccines under this measure shall: 1. Screen each patient for contraindications and precautions consistent with current guidelines of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices or, where applicable, the recognized medical professional organizations designated under state law; 2. Provide each patient or the patient's parent or guardian with the current Vaccine Information Statement (VIS) published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or the equivalent FDA-required fact sheet for vaccines administered under Emergency Use Authorization; 3. Obtain informed consent from the patient, or from the parent or legal guardian of a minor patient, prior to administration; 4. Administer vaccines in a manner consistent with the manufacturer's labeling and applicable clinical guidelines; 5. Observe the patient for a minimum of fifteen minutes following administration for signs of adverse reaction; and 6. Maintain appropriate emergency supplies, including epinephrine, at the site of administration. (b) In the event of a significant adverse reaction, the qualified pharmacist shall: 1. Provide immediate appropriate medical intervention; 2. Arrange for transport to an emergency medical facility if clinically indicated; 3. Report the adverse event to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) in accordance with federal requirements; and 4. Notify the patient's primary care provider, if known, within forty-eight hours. Section 6. Documentation and Reporting (a) A qualified pharmacist who administers a vaccine under this measure shall, within twenty-four hours of administration, report the following information to the immunization registry: 1. The name, date of birth, and address of the patient; 2. The name, manufacturer, lot number, and expiration date of the vaccine administered; 3. The date, route, and anatomic site of administration; 4. The name and license number of the administering pharmacist; and 5. The name and address of the pharmacy at which the vaccine was administered. (b) A qualified pharmacist shall make reasonable efforts to notify the patient's primary care provider of the vaccination within thirty days of administration, using electronic health information exchange where available. (c) The pharmacy shall maintain records of all vaccines administered pursuant to this measure for a period of not less than seven years, or as otherwise required by the board. Section 7. Insurance Coverage and Reimbursement (a) No health plan, insurer, or managed care organization operating in this state shall: 1. Require prior authorization for vaccines administered by a qualified pharmacist in accordance with this measure; 2. Impose cost-sharing requirements for pharmacist-administered vaccines that exceed cost-sharing requirements for the same vaccines administered by a physician; or 3. Exclude pharmacist-administered vaccines from coverage that would otherwise apply if the vaccine were administered by a physician. (b) Reimbursement rates for pharmacist-administered vaccines shall be no less than the rates established for vaccine administration under the state Medicaid program, or the applicable Medicare Part D rate, whichever is greater. Section 8. Rulemaking (a) The board, in consultation with the department and the state medical board, shall promulgate rules necessary to implement this measure within one hundred eighty days of its effective date, including but not limited to: 1. Application and verification procedures for qualified pharmacist designation; 2. Standards for standing orders applicable to vaccination of individuals aged three through six years; 3. Record-keeping and inspection requirements; and 4. Procedures for investigating and addressing complaints related to pharmacist-administered vaccination. Section 9. Preemption (a) This measure shall preempt any local ordinance, regulation, or rule that restricts or limits the authority of a qualified pharmacist to administer vaccines as authorized under this measure. (b) Nothing in this measure shall be construed to preempt any more permissive local ordinance, regulation, or rule that expands access to pharmacist-administered vaccination beyond the provisions of this measure. Section 10. Severability If any provision of this measure, or its application to any person or circumstance, is held invalid, the invalidity does not affect other provisions or applications of this measure that can be given effect without the invalid provision or application, and to this end the provisions of this measure are severable. Section 11. Effective Date This measure shall take effect on [DATE], or upon passage and approval, whichever is later. Policy Considerations This model legislation represents one approach to permanently expanding pharmacist vaccination authority. Legislators considering this template should evaluate: - Scope of practice boundaries and physician oversight requirements, particularly for vaccination of young children aged three through six where pediatric clinical judgment may be especially important - Liability and malpractice insurance implications for pharmacists administering a broader range of vaccines, and whether existing pharmacy liability frameworks adequately address expanded duties - The impact on care coordination when vaccinations occur outside the primary care setting, including the reliability of notification mechanisms to patients' primary care providers - Fiscal impact on state budgets and healthcare systems - Compatibility with existing state statutes and regulatory frameworks The SAFE Research Institute presents this material as an educational resource and does not advocate for or against any specific legislative outcome. --- This document is provided by the SAFE Research Institute as an educational resource. It is not legal advice. It is offered to inform analysis and discussion, not to promote the adoption of any particular measure. Readers should consult qualified professionals regarding their existing statutory frameworks, constitutional provisions, and administrative procedures.

title: Equitable Immunization Access: A Policy Analysis
summary: Requires state health departments to identify and address immunization deserts, mandates the establishment of mobile vaccination units, community health worker immunization programs, and multilingual outreach initiatives to eliminate disparities in vaccination rates based on race, income, geography, and language.
text: Educational example, not proposed legislation. This document is provided by the SAFE Research Institute for educational analysis of how a policy approach might be structured. It is not a bill, and its inclusion here is not a recommendation to adopt any measure. This educational example examines an approach relating to public health; requiring the identification and remediation of immunization deserts; establishing mobile vaccination programs, community health worker initiatives, and multilingual outreach; creating the Immunization Equity Fund; and providing for related matters. Section 1. Purpose and Findings (a) This example is premised on the following findings: 1. Immunization is a cornerstone of public health, yet significant disparities in vaccination rates persist across the state based on race, ethnicity, household income, geographic location, and primary language. 2. Data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state immunization registries indicate that communities of color, rural populations, and low-income households often experience lower vaccination rates for routine childhood, adolescent, and adult immunizations compared to state and national averages. 3. Geographic analysis reveals that many areas of the state qualify as immunization deserts, defined as communities where residents face significant barriers to accessing vaccination services due to distance, provider scarcity, transportation limitations, or inadequate culturally and linguistically appropriate services. 4. The COVID-19 pandemic further exposed and exacerbated existing immunization disparities, with Black, Latino, Indigenous, and rural communities experiencing disproportionately lower vaccination rates and higher rates of vaccine-preventable morbidity and mortality. 5. Evidence-based interventions, including mobile vaccination units, community health worker programs, and multilingual outreach campaigns, have been associated with improved vaccination rates in underserved populations when implemented with sustained funding and community engagement. 6. Multiple states and localities have successfully piloted or permanently funded programs to address immunization deserts, providing replicable models for statewide implementation. 7. It is in the interest of the state to systematically identify and address immunization deserts and to eliminate disparities in immunization access to protect the health of all residents. (b) The purpose of this measure is to establish a comprehensive framework for identifying immunization deserts, deploying targeted interventions to improve immunization access in underserved communities, and eliminating disparities in vaccination rates based on race, ethnicity, income, geography, and language. Section 2. Definitions As used in this measure: 1. "Community health worker" means a frontline public health worker who is a trusted member of, or has an unusually close understanding of, the community served, and who serves as a liaison between health services and the community to facilitate access to services, improve the quality and cultural competence of service delivery, and promote health equity. 2. "Department" means the state department of health or its successor agency. 3. "Director" means the director of the department or the director's designee. 4. "Federally qualified health center" means an entity that has been designated as a federally qualified health center under Section 330 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 254b). 5. "Immunization desert" means a geographic area designated by the department under Section 3 of this measure in which residents face significant barriers to accessing immunization services. 6. "Immunization Equity Fund" means the fund established under Section 8 of this measure. 7. "Immunization registry" means the statewide immunization information system maintained by the department for the purpose of recording and tracking vaccine administration. 8. "Limited English proficiency" means the inability to adequately understand or communicate effectively in English, as determined by standards established by the department. 9. "Local health department" means a county, municipal, or regional health department or district operating within the state. 10. "Mobile vaccination unit" means a vehicle, temporary facility, or portable clinic equipped and staffed to administer vaccines at locations outside of traditional health care settings. 11. "Underserved population" means a population group that experiences disparities in immunization coverage rates due to barriers including but not limited to geographic isolation, poverty, lack of health insurance, racial or ethnic discrimination, disability, homelessness, or limited English proficiency. Section 3. Identification of Immunization Deserts (a) The department shall, within one hundred eighty days of the effective date of this measure and annually thereafter, conduct a comprehensive assessment to identify immunization deserts within the state. The assessment shall consider: 1. Geographic distribution of immunization providers, including physicians, pharmacies, federally qualified health centers, local health departments, and other entities authorized to administer vaccines; 2. Travel time and distance from population centers to the nearest immunization provider, with particular attention to public transportation availability; 3. Immunization coverage rates disaggregated by census tract, zip code, county, race, ethnicity, age group, and insurance status, utilizing data from the immunization registry, the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, and other available data sources; 4. Socioeconomic indicators including poverty rates, rates of uninsurance and underinsurance, and rates of limited English proficiency; 5. Availability of culturally and linguistically appropriate immunization services; and 6. Input from community organizations, local health departments, and residents of potentially affected communities. (b) The department shall designate as an immunization desert any geographic area that meets one or more of the following criteria: 1. The area has an immunization coverage rate for any routinely recommended vaccine that is more than ten percentage points below the statewide average for the relevant age group; 2. Residents of the area must travel more than thirty minutes by available transportation to reach the nearest immunization provider; 3. The ratio of immunization providers to population within the area falls below a threshold established by the department by regulation; or 4. The area demonstrates a pattern of persistent immunization disparities affecting underserved populations, as determined by the department based on the assessment conducted under subsection (a). (c) The department shall publish a map of designated immunization deserts on its website, updated annually, and shall submit a report of its findings and designations to the Governor and the Legislature. Section 4. Mobile Vaccination Unit Program (a) The department shall establish and administer a Mobile Vaccination Unit Program to deliver immunization services directly to communities within designated immunization deserts. (b) The program shall: 1. Deploy not fewer than one mobile vaccination unit per designated immunization desert, or per region containing multiple adjacent immunization deserts, within twelve months of the designation; 2. Operate mobile vaccination units on a regular, predictable schedule, with each designated immunization desert receiving service not less than twice per month; 3. Offer all routinely recommended vaccines for children, adolescents, and adults, as established by the state immunization schedule; 4. Provide immunization services at no cost to uninsured and underinsured individuals, utilizing Vaccines for Children program stock, state-purchased vaccine, and other available resources; 5. Staff each mobile vaccination unit with at least one licensed health care provider authorized to administer vaccines and at least one community health worker or patient navigator; 6. Coordinate with local health departments, schools, houses of worship, community organizations, employers, and other community-based institutions to identify optimal deployment locations and schedules; and 7. Maintain supplies and equipment necessary for proper vaccine storage, administration, and management of adverse events. (c) The department may contract with local health departments, federally qualified health centers, hospital systems, pharmacy organizations, or other qualified entities to operate mobile vaccination units under this section. (d) The department shall maintain records of all vaccines administered through the Mobile Vaccination Unit Program and shall report program data to the immunization registry in accordance with existing state law. Section 5. Community Health Worker Immunization Program (a) The department shall establish a Community Health Worker Immunization Program to employ and deploy community health workers in designated immunization deserts for the purpose of improving immunization awareness, education, and uptake. (b) Community health workers employed or contracted under this program shall: 1. Conduct door-to-door and community-based outreach to identify unvaccinated and undervaccinated individuals; 2. Provide culturally appropriate education regarding the safety, efficacy, and benefits of recommended immunizations; 3. Assist individuals in scheduling vaccination appointments, obtaining transportation to immunization providers, and navigating insurance coverage and financial assistance programs; 4. Address vaccine hesitancy through evidence-based motivational interviewing and trusted messenger strategies; 5. Provide follow-up to ensure completion of multi-dose vaccine series; 6. Collect and report data on barriers to immunization identified through community engagement; and 7. Serve as liaisons between underserved communities and the formal health care system. (c) The department shall establish training requirements for community health workers participating in this program, which shall include, at minimum: 1. Overview of the recommended immunization schedules and the diseases they prevent; 2. Evidence-based techniques for addressing vaccine hesitancy and misinformation; 3. Cultural competency and health literacy principles; 4. Privacy and confidentiality requirements under state and federal law; and 5. Documentation and reporting requirements. (d) The department shall prioritize the recruitment and hiring of community health workers who are members of the underserved populations and communities they will serve, including individuals who are bilingual or multilingual. Section 6. Multilingual Outreach and Communication (a) The department shall develop and implement a comprehensive multilingual immunization outreach and communication strategy that includes: 1. Translation of all immunization-related educational materials, including vaccine information statements, appointment scheduling tools, consent forms, and public awareness campaigns, into the ten most commonly spoken non-English languages in the state, as determined by the most recent data from the American Community Survey; 2. Provision of interpreter services, including telephonic and in-person interpretation, at all state-operated and state-funded immunization sites for individuals with limited English proficiency; 3. Development of culturally adapted immunization awareness campaigns that are designed in partnership with community organizations representing underserved populations and that utilize trusted community channels including ethnic media, community radio, social media platforms, and faith-based organizations; 4. Establishment of a multilingual immunization information hotline, staffed during regular business hours, to provide vaccine information, assist with appointment scheduling, and connect callers with community health workers; and 5. Collaboration with school districts, Head Start programs, and childcare providers serving communities with high rates of limited English proficiency to distribute immunization information and facilitate vaccination. (b) The department shall ensure that all public-facing digital platforms and web-based tools related to immunization, including the immunization registry portal and online appointment scheduling systems, are accessible in the languages identified under subsection (a)(1) and comply with applicable accessibility standards. Section 7. Data Collection and Accountability (a) The department shall collect, analyze, and publish data annually on immunization coverage rates disaggregated by: 1. Race and ethnicity; 2. Age group; 3. Geographic area, including by county and census tract; 4. Insurance status; 5. Primary language; and 6. Household income, to the extent such data is available. (b) The department shall establish measurable goals for eliminating immunization disparities in designated immunization deserts, including: 1. Achieving immunization coverage rates within five percentage points of the statewide average for all routinely recommended vaccines in each designated immunization desert within three years of designation; 2. Reducing racial and ethnic disparities in immunization coverage by fifty percent within five years of the effective date of this measure; and 3. Ensuring that no geographic area of the state qualifies as an immunization desert within seven years of the effective date of this measure. (c) The department shall submit a biennial report to the Governor and the Legislature on progress toward the goals established under subsection (b), including an assessment of the effectiveness of the programs established under this measure and recommendations for additional legislative or administrative action. (d) The department shall convene an Immunization Equity Advisory Council, composed of representatives of underserved populations, community health workers, local health department officials, immunization providers, and public health researchers, to advise the department on the implementation and evaluation of programs under this measure. Section 8. Immunization Equity Fund (a) There is hereby created in the state treasury a special fund to be known as the Immunization Equity Fund. (b) The fund shall consist of: 1. Appropriations made by the Legislature for the purposes of this measure; 2. Federal grants and funds allocated to the state for immunization equity, access, or outreach purposes; 3. Donations, gifts, and bequests made to the fund; and 4. Any other funds designated by law for deposit into the fund. (c) Moneys in the fund shall be used exclusively for: 1. Operation of the Mobile Vaccination Unit Program established under Section 4; 2. Operation of the Community Health Worker Immunization Program established under Section 5; 3. Multilingual outreach and communication activities under Section 6; 4. Data collection, analysis, and reporting under Section 7; 5. Vaccine purchase for uninsured and underinsured individuals in designated immunization deserts; and 6. Administrative costs directly associated with the programs established under this measure, not to exceed ten percent of total annual fund expenditures. (d) The department shall publish an annual accounting of all expenditures from the fund on its website. Section 9. Non-Discrimination (a) No program or service established under this measure shall discriminate against any individual on the basis of race, color, national origin, sex, age, disability, religion, sexual orientation, gender identity, immigration status, or primary language. (b) Immunization services provided under this measure shall be available to all eligible individuals regardless of insurance status, ability to pay, or documentation of citizenship or immigration status. Section 10. Coordination with Existing Programs (a) The department shall coordinate the implementation of this measure with existing federal, state, and local immunization programs, including but not limited to: 1. The Vaccines for Children (VFC) program; 2. The Section 317 Immunization Program; 3. Programs administered by federally qualified health centers; 4. School-based health programs; and 5. Maternal and child health programs. (b) Nothing in this measure shall be construed to duplicate, supplant, or reduce funding for existing immunization programs. Section 11. Severability If any provision of this measure, or its application to any person or circumstance, is held invalid, the invalidity does not affect other provisions or applications of this measure that can be given effect without the invalid provision or application, and to this end the provisions of this measure are severable. Section 12. Effective Date This measure shall take effect on [DATE], or upon passage and approval, whichever is later. Policy Considerations This model legislation represents one approach to addressing geographic and demographic disparities in immunization access. Legislators considering this template should evaluate: - Whether designated immunization desert criteria appropriately reflect local conditions, given wide variation in rural versus urban healthcare infrastructure across states - The fiscal impact of establishing and sustaining mobile vaccination units, community health worker programs, and multilingual outreach at scale, including ongoing operational costs beyond initial appropriations - Potential overlap or conflict with existing federal programs such as Vaccines for Children (VFC) and Section 317, and whether state funds would supplement or inadvertently duplicate federal resources - Fiscal impact on state budgets and healthcare systems - Compatibility with existing state statutes and regulatory frameworks The SAFE Research Institute presents this material as an educational resource and does not advocate for or against any specific legislative outcome. --- This document is provided by the SAFE Research Institute as an educational resource. title: Insurance Coverage for Immunizations: A Policy Analysis
summary: Requires all state-regulated health insurance plans to provide coverage for immunizations recommended by the state health department without cost-sharing, copayments, or prior authorization, ensuring no resident faces financial barriers to vaccination.
text: Educational example, not proposed legislation. This document is provided by the SAFE Research Institute for educational analysis of how a policy approach might be structured. It is not a bill, and its inclusion here is not a recommendation to adopt any measure. This educational example examines an approach relating to health insurance; requiring coverage of state-recommended immunizations without cost-sharing; establishing provider reimbursement standards; and providing for enforcement and related matters. Section 1. Purpose The Legislature finds that financial barriers to immunization, including copayments, deductibles, and prior authorization requirements, reduce vaccination rates and disproportionately affect low-income families, older adults, and medically underserved populations. This measure ensures that all residents covered by state-regulated health insurance plans can receive recommended immunizations without encountering cost barriers at the point of care. Section 2. Definitions As used in this measure: 1. "Cost-sharing" means any copayment, coinsurance, deductible, or other out-of-pocket expense imposed on an enrollee at the time an immunization service is rendered. 2. "Covered immunization" means any vaccine or combination of vaccines included on the immunization schedule published by the state department of health, including those administered for routine, catch-up, or risk-based indications. 3. "Health benefit plan" means any individual or group health insurance policy, health care service plan contract, or managed care plan issued, delivered, or renewed in this state, including plans offered through the state health benefit exchange. This term does not include excepted benefit plans, short-term limited duration insurance, or plans administered by a federal agency. 4. "Issuer" means any health insurance company, health care service plan, or managed care organization authorized to transact business in this state. 5. "Administering provider" means any health care professional or facility authorized under state law to administer vaccines, including physicians, advanced practice providers, pharmacists, and pharmacies. Section 3. Coverage Requirements (a) Every health benefit plan issued, delivered, amended, or renewed in this state on or after the effective date of this measure shall provide coverage for all covered immunizations. (b) Coverage shall include the vaccine product, its administration, and any related office visit or clinical evaluation necessary for the immunization to be provided, when the immunization is the primary purpose of the visit. (c) Coverage shall extend to immunizations administered by any administering provider acting within their scope of practice, regardless of whether the provider is within the plan's contracted network. Section 4. Prohibited Cost-Sharing (a) No issuer shall impose any cost-sharing on an enrollee for a covered immunization, regardless of whether the immunization is provided by an in-network or out-of-network administering provider. (b) No issuer shall require prior authorization, step therapy, or any other utilization management technique as a condition of coverage for a covered immunization. (c) No issuer shall apply any annual or lifetime limit specific to immunization benefits under this measure. (d) An issuer shall not classify immunization services under a separate benefit tier or category that results in less favorable coverage than other preventive services. Section 5. Provider Reimbursement Standards (a) Issuers shall reimburse administering providers for covered immunizations at a rate not less than the applicable rate published under the Medicare Part B physician fee schedule, or the rate negotiated under the provider's contract with the issuer, whichever is greater. (b) For out-of-network administering providers, issuers shall reimburse at not less than one hundred percent of the Medicare Part B rate for the vaccine product and its administration. (c) Reimbursement shall be rendered within thirty calendar days of submission of a clean claim. Section 6. Pharmacy Administration Coverage (a) Issuers shall provide coverage for immunizations administered at licensed pharmacies on the same terms and conditions as immunizations administered in a physician's office. (b) No issuer shall require an enrollee to obtain a prescription as a condition of coverage for a vaccine that may be lawfully administered by a pharmacist under state pharmacy practice laws. (c) Pharmacies shall be reimbursed for both the vaccine product and a reasonable administration fee, which shall not be less than the administration fee established under the Medicare Part D vaccine program. Section 7. Implementation Timeline (a) This measure shall apply to all health benefit plans issued or renewed on or after January 1 of the calendar year following enactment. (b) Issuers shall update their formularies, provider communications, and claims processing systems to comply with this measure within one hundred eighty days of enactment. (c) The department of insurance shall issue guidance to issuers regarding compliance with this measure within ninety days of enactment. Section 8. Enforcement (a) The department of insurance shall enforce this measure and may examine issuer compliance as part of routine market conduct examinations. (b) Any issuer found in violation of this measure shall be subject to corrective action, including: 1. An order to provide retroactive reimbursement to affected enrollees for any improperly assessed cost-sharing; 2. A civil penalty of not more than one thousand dollars per violation per enrollee; 3. Suspension or revocation of the issuer's certificate of authority for repeated or willful violations. (c) An enrollee aggrieved by a violation of this measure may file a complaint with the department of insurance and shall have a private right of action to recover actual damages, reasonable attorney fees, and costs. Policy Considerations This model legislation represents one approach to eliminating cost-sharing barriers for immunization services. Legislators considering this template should evaluate: - The impact on insurance premiums and overall healthcare costs, as mandated zero cost-sharing benefits are ultimately distributed across the insured risk pool - Whether requiring coverage of out-of-network immunization providers at Medicare rates creates adequate reimbursement or may lead to provider access issues in some markets - The interaction with federal ACA preventive services mandates and ERISA preemption, which limits the applicability of state insurance mandates to self-funded employer plans - Fiscal impact on state budgets and healthcare systems - Compatibility with existing state statutes and regulatory frameworks The SAFE Research Institute presents this material as an educational resource and does not advocate for or against any specific legislative outcome. --- This document is provided by the SAFE Research Institute as an educational resource. title: Medical-Only Immunization Exemption Standards: A Policy Analysis
summary: Establishes medical-only exemption standards for school and childcare immunization requirements, permitting only physician-certified medical exemptions from vaccination schedules.
text: Educational example, not proposed legislation. This document is provided by the SAFE Research Institute for educational analysis of how a policy approach might be structured. It is not a bill, and its inclusion here is not a recommendation to adopt any measure. Section 1: Purpose and Findings (a) This example is premised on the following findings: (1) Childhood immunization is one of the most effective public health interventions in modern medicine, preventing millions of cases of serious illness and death annually. (2) Research has documented an association between medical-only exemption standards and higher childhood vaccination rates. For example, CDC kindergarten vaccination surveys for the 2023–24 school year reported that West Virginia, which at that time limited exemptions to medical grounds, was among the states with the highest MMR coverage, at approximately 98 percent, alongside a very low non-medical exemption rate. State exemption laws continue to change through legislation, executive action, and litigation, and current requirements vary by state. (3) In 2015, following a measles outbreak linked to Disneyland in Anaheim, California, the California Legislature enacted SB 277, eliminating personal belief exemptions from school immunization requirements. Vaccination rates increased measurably in the years following enactment. (4) Only a small number of states currently limit school and childcare immunization exemptions to medical grounds. The specific states in this group have shifted in recent years as a result of new legislation, executive action, and court decisions, and legislators should confirm the current status of any comparison state before relying on it. (5) Peer-reviewed research has documented an association between broader availability of non-medical exemptions and the geographic clustering of under-vaccinated individuals, which studies have in turn linked to outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases such as measles and pertussis (whooping cough). (6) It is the purpose of this measure to protect children and the public health by ensuring that only medically justified exemptions are permitted from school and childcare immunization requirements. Section 2: Definitions As used in this measure: (a) "Immunization requirements" means the vaccinations required by the State Department of Health for enrollment in any school or childcare facility, as established by rule in accordance with recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP). (b) "Medical exemption" means an exemption from one or more required immunizations granted on the basis of a licensed physician's certification that a specific vaccine is medically contraindicated or poses a significant health risk for an individual child. (c) "Licensed physician" means a person holding a current, unrestricted license to practice medicine issued by the State Board of Medical Examiners, holding the degree of Doctor of Medicine (M.D.) or Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (D.O.). (d) "School" means any public or private institution providing instruction in grades pre-kindergarten through twelve, including charter schools and virtual academies requiring any in-person attendance. (e) "Childcare facility" means any licensed or registered facility providing care, supervision, or instruction to children under six years of age outside the child's home. Section 3: Elimination of Non-Medical Exemptions (a) No exemption from the immunization requirements of this State based upon personal, philosophical, moral, or religious beliefs shall be recognized for purposes of enrollment in any school or childcare facility. (b) The sole exemption from immunization requirements for school or childcare enrollment shall be a medical exemption issued in accordance with Section 4 of this measure. (c) Any existing statute, regulation, or administrative rule permitting non-medical exemptions from school or childcare immunization requirements is hereby superseded to the extent of any conflict with this measure. Section 4: Medical Exemption Standards (a) A medical exemption shall be valid only if certified by a licensed physician on a form prescribed by the State Department of Health. (b) The certification shall specify: (1) The specific vaccine or vaccines for which the exemption is sought; (2) The medical condition or conditions that contraindicate administration of each such vaccine; and (3) Whether the exemption is temporary or permanent in nature, and, if temporary, the expected duration. (c) All medical exemptions shall be subject to annual renewal. The licensed physician must recertify the continuing medical necessity of the exemption each year prior to the start of the school term. (d) The State Department of Health shall review medical exemptions and may request additional documentation or refer cases for independent medical review where the rate of exemptions issued by a single physician exceeds a threshold established by departmental rule. Section 5: Conditional Enrollment (a) A child who has not received all required immunizations but who is not seeking an exemption may enroll conditionally in a school or childcare facility, provided the child: (1) Has received at least the first dose of each required vaccine series; and (2) Is on an active catch-up schedule to complete all remaining doses in accordance with the immunization timeline recommended by the State Department of Health. (b) Conditional enrollment shall be reviewed at intervals not to exceed ninety (90) days. A child who fails to remain current with the approved catch-up schedule shall be excluded from attendance until compliance is restored. Section 6: Public Education and Outreach (a) The State Department of Health shall develop and fund a comprehensive public education program to inform parents, guardians, and healthcare providers about immunization requirements, the safety and efficacy of vaccines, and the provisions of this measure. (b) The program shall include culturally and linguistically appropriate materials and shall prioritize outreach to communities with historically low vaccination rates. (c) The State shall make available, at no cost to the family, all vaccines required under the immunization schedule for children who are uninsured or underinsured. Section 7: Severability If any provision of this measure, or the application thereof to any person or circumstance, is held invalid by a court of competent jurisdiction, the invalidity shall not affect other provisions or applications of this measure that can be given effect without the invalid provision or application, and to this end the provisions of this measure are severable. Section 8: Effective Date This measure shall take effect on the first day of the school year immediately following the date of enactment, provided that no fewer than one hundred and eighty (180) days have elapsed between the date of enactment and such first day. If fewer than one hundred and eighty days remain before the start of the next school year, this measure shall take effect on the first day of the subsequent school year. Policy Considerations This model legislation represents one approach to standardizing immunization exemption policies for school and childcare entry. Legislators considering this template should evaluate: - Constitutional and legal challenges related to the elimination of religious exemptions, including First Amendment free exercise claims and state Religious Freedom Restoration Act statutes that may apply in some jurisdictions - The impact on families who hold sincere religious or philosophical objections, and whether alternative accommodations such as homeschool provisions adequately address their concerns - Whether the medical exemption review process imposes undue burdens on physicians or creates barriers for children with legitimate but uncommon contraindications - Fiscal impact on state budgets and healthcare systems - Compatibility with existing state statutes and regulatory frameworks The SAFE Research Institute presents this material as an educational resource and does not advocate for or against any specific legislative outcome. The elimination of non-medical exemptions is among the most contested issues in immunization policy, raising significant constitutional and religious-liberty questions; this template is provided to inform analysis of one approach, not to endorse it. --- This document is provided by the SAFE Research Institute as an educational resource. It is not legal advice. It is offered to inform analysis and discussion, not to promote the adoption of any particular measure. title: Interstate Public Health Collaboration: An Educational Overview
summary: Affirms the state legislature's support for interstate public health collaborations involving shared epidemiological data, coordinated immunization guidance, and joint emergency preparedness planning among participating states.
text: About this document. The following is an annotated example of resolution language, provided for educational illustration of how a state legislature might formally express support for interstate public health cooperation. It is offered as a template for study and adaptation, not as a recommendation by the SAFE Research Institute that any legislature adopt it or take any particular action. Resolution drafting conventions ("WHEREAS… NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED") are reproduced here so readers can see how such instruments are typically structured. A RESOLUTION affirming the commitment of the State of [STATE] to interstate cooperation in maintaining evidence-based public health standards, epidemiological surveillance, and emergency preparedness. Introduced by [SPONSOR(S)] --- WHEREAS, the protection of public health is a fundamental responsibility of state government, grounded in the police power reserved to the states under the Tenth Amendment to the United States Constitution; and WHEREAS, infectious diseases do not respect state boundaries, and the effective prevention and control of communicable disease requires coordinated action among jurisdictions; and WHEREAS, states have collaborated on matters of public health through mechanisms such as interstate compacts, mutual aid agreements, and regional health partnerships; and WHEREAS, more recent regional public health alliances, such as the West Coast Health Alliance, formed in 2025 among California, Oregon, Washington, and Hawaii, reflect growing interest in multi-state coordination on evidence-based immunization guidance, the sharing of epidemiological surveillance data, and public health laboratory capacity; and WHEREAS, disruptions to federal public health advisory processes, reductions in federal epidemiological capacity, or delays in federal immunization guidance may create gaps in public health protection that states must be prepared to address collectively; and WHEREAS, the sharing of real-time epidemiological data among states enables earlier detection of disease outbreaks, more accurate risk assessment, and more effective deployment of countermeasures; and WHEREAS, coordinated interstate procurement of vaccines and public health supplies can reduce costs, ensure equitable distribution, and strengthen supply chain resilience for all participating states; and WHEREAS, the residents of this state benefit when neighboring and allied states maintain robust immunization programs, as high regional vaccination coverage reduces the risk of disease importation and interstate transmission; and WHEREAS, interstate public health collaboration strengthens the capacity of each participating state while respecting the sovereignty and legislative authority of every jurisdiction involved; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the [Legislature/General Assembly/General Court] of the State of [STATE]: Section 1. That this body affirms its support for the participation of the State of [STATE] in interstate public health collaborations, compacts, and agreements that advance evidence-based immunization practice and communicable disease prevention. Section 2. That the state department of health is encouraged to enter into memoranda of understanding or data-sharing agreements with counterpart agencies in other states for the purpose of: (a) Sharing epidemiological surveillance data, including immunization coverage rates, disease incidence reports, and outbreak investigation findings; (b) Coordinating evidence-based immunization schedules informed by the guidance of recognized medical professional organizations; (c) Establishing joint procurement arrangements for vaccines and public health supplies to improve cost efficiency and supply chain reliability; (d) Conducting collaborative public health workforce training and emergency preparedness exercises. Section 3. That the governor is encouraged to designate a representative to participate in regional and national forums dedicated to interstate public health coordination, and to report annually to the legislature on the status and outcomes of such collaborations. Section 4. That nothing in this resolution shall be construed to cede the legislative authority of this state, to bind this state to any obligation requiring the expenditure of funds not otherwise appropriated, or to supersede any existing state law or regulation. Section 5. That copies of this resolution shall be transmitted to the governor, the director of the state department of health, and the presiding officers of the legislatures of every other state. Policy Considerations This model resolution represents one approach to formalizing interstate public health cooperation. Legislators considering this template should evaluate: - Implications for state sovereignty and legislative authority when entering data-sharing agreements or joint procurement arrangements with other states - Privacy and data security considerations when sharing epidemiological surveillance data across state lines, including compatibility with varying state health information privacy laws - Whether joint procurement arrangements may conflict with existing state procurement statutes or create dependencies on other states' purchasing decisions - Fiscal impact on state budgets and healthcare systems - Compatibility with existing state statutes and regulatory frameworks The SAFE Research Institute presents this material as an educational resource and does not advocate for or against any specific legislative outcome. The resolution text above is an illustrative example of legislative drafting, reproduced for study; its inclusion here is not an endorsement of its adoption. --- This document is provided by the SAFE Research Institute as an educational resource.
